# Abstract

# Introduction

Fish populations are one of the last wild resources managed globally. Not only are they a key source of wild food, they are an economic driver, contribution $X annually. This motivates the collection of extensive data on these wild populations and while fish populations are hard to study, some core ecological concepts have been derived from data collected on fish populations (e.g., match-mismatch hypothesis). The need to predict the future of these populations and identify levels of sustainable use often spurrs efforts to collect information on the age structure of the population and the composition of ages in fisheries. As such, it has become commonplace for the field of fisheries science and management to apply age-structured models to study their population ecology and demography, which enables better predictions of population size under varying levels of fisheries removals.

Age-structured models applied in fisheries science found its roots in the Leslie matrix, and they began to be commonly applied in the 1960s when computers made large matrix calculations piratical. Methods have continued to advance, but a basic cohort equation lies at the core of all age-structured stock assessment models. Indeed, age-structured models may be the most actively used in the field of fisheries science.

The active and common use of such models have contributed to a continued evolution of methods and tools, starting from aspict to apply virtual population analyses (VPA), to Stock Synthesis and a4a to apply statistical catch at age (SCAA), to state-space approaches enabled by WHAM and SAM. Consequently, the field has been at the forefront of statistical and programmatic advancement, introducing tools such as TMB and RTMB that have been applicable well beyond the field of fisheries science. However, one difficulty that practitioners may face is that the learning curve behind these methods is steep. It requires a high bar of statistical and programmatic knowledge. Yet at the core of these models are true questions of population ecologists. There are likely ideas that biologists and ecologists have that they want to apply to age-structured analyses, yet the statistical and programmatic requirements act as a barrier to the testing of their ideas.

Here we introduce a tiny assessment model, `tinyAM`, which is an R package designed to make age-structured stock assessment models more accessible. Ultimately, assessment models express hypotheses about where unexplained variation arises: recruitment, abundance deviations, fishing mortality, natural mortality, or monitoring program gaps or sampling errors. This framework lets users change one or more assumption to examine their consequences using the same diagnostic, simulation, and forecasting tools. The interface is designed to be expressive and intuitive, leveraging principles of tidy data, the flexibility of R formulas, and the use of print methods and interactive visuals via `plotly` and `flesdashboard` to rapidly develop and compare multiple models. The 'tidy' prefix refers to a small modeling vocabulary where complexity emerges from combining understandable components rather than choosing among many special-purpose models. The overall goal is to make age-structured assessment models more accessible to biologists and ecologists; though they may not have extensive statistical and programming traing, they understand the fundamentals of population ecology and work in the tidyverse and are familiar with R packages like glmmTMB.

## Introduction

- Acknowledge the closest precedents. a4a uses R formulas to specify age-structured assessments [@jardim2015]. WHAM spans statistical catch-at-age and state-space models and supports comparisons among them [@stock2021]. SAM and Stock Synthesis are established assessment frameworks [@nielsen2014; @methot2013].
- State tinyAM’s design goal. A biologist or ecologist with basic R skills can express an assumption in a short model call, see where it enters the model and inspect how it affects the fit, forecasts and stock estimates. ### Northern cod worked example

**Biological question.** Does allowing natural mortality to vary over time improve predictions of Northern cod survey observations at age and change the inferred history of spawning-stock biomass (SSB)? The [2025 Northern cod assessment](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2026/mpo-dfo/fs70-5/Fs70-5-2026-026-eng.pdf) motivates the question through its analysis of natural mortality and prey availability. The worked example uses the packaged catch and survey observations to evaluate the more specific assumption about variation in mortality.

**Specify two alternatives.** Start with the NCAM-like fit in [the case-study script](https://github.com/PaulRegular/tinyAM/blob/694039bb4ba31a2419dc587098442ed05ba7af91/analysis/case_study/001_models.R), which uses 1983–2025 and ages 2–14+. Compare fixed natural mortality of 0.3 per year with deviations around `log(0.3)` that are correlated across years and age blocks. Retain the same data, recruitment, cohort survival, fishing mortality and observation specifications. Show the mortality settings and how they enter cohort survival. Use the existing SCAA-, SAM- and NCAM-like fits in the supplement to show how several components can vary together.

```r
m_varying <- ncam
m_constant <- update(ncam, M_settings = list(process = "off"))
```

**Evaluate the hypothesis.** Use `plot_model()` to verify the change in specification and `check_tam()` to assess numerical fit and uncertainty. Inspect age-by-year survey residuals for runs of over- or underprediction. Compare one-year-ahead survey log-RMSE and MASE on identical forecast origins and survey–age observations. Both hindcasts condition on observed aggregate catch. Report the full fold coverage and failures before interpreting score differences.

**Interpret the consequences.** Compare estimated mortality and SSB with uncertainty, and use retrospective peels to assess how terminal estimates change as observations are removed. Examine whether the mortality process is weakly estimated or near a correlation boundary. Interpret any predictive improvement relative to the chosen constant mortality baseline. Discuss what external information on survival, fishing mortality or availability would help distinguish explanations.
